vignette: The rain had turned the Pacific Coast highway into a slick mirror that night, and Kaleo had been driving home from his sister's fiftieth birthday in Kaneohe. He remembered the sudden flare of high beams cutting through the downpour, the sickening lurch of his sedan losing traction, and the violent percussion of the guardrail giving way. Metal screamed as the car spun and struck the embankment. The airbag detonated, dusting his face with white powder, while a cracked cup holder and a spilled tumbler of amber liquor from the passenger seat flooded the cabin with the sharp, sweet sting of bourbon. He lay pinned for nearly an hour before fire responders cut the roof free, his left shoulder and ribs burning where the seatbelt had dug in, his body rigid, hands still twisted at the ten-and-two position as if still holding the wheel. In the weeks that followed, Kaleo found that the crash never truly left him. When a memory of the impact surfaced, it did not arrive as a distant photograph. What frightened him most was how completely real it became across all his senses at once: the glare of headlights, the hiss of escaping coolant, the thick odor of alcohol and burnt rubber, the crushing pressure against his chest. His body remembered too. As soon as the recollection tightened in his mind, his shoulders would hike forward, his hands would curl into fists on his lap, and the familiar, sharp ache would flare in his ribs and left shoulder, exactly where the steel had held him fast. He had come to believe that if he could just keep those memories from rising, he would finally be safe. So he began to map his days around what he could control. He stopped driving past the interchange where wrecks frequently drew crowds of rubbernecks, and when he saw a mangled sedan or a tow truck winching a crushed hood, his throat would constrict and he would look away, his breathing quickening. The smell of liquor on a man's breath at a local market made him step backward, certain that another spill was imminent. At his fabrication shop in the Industrial District, where his work as a welder kept him knee-deep in steel frames and ozone, he grew hyperaware of the low, guttural idle of delivery trucks backing up near the loading bay. The rumble of engines and the screech of air brakes triggered a sudden stillness, his gaze fixed on the concrete floor as he waited for the noise to pass. He began routing his break walks away from the bay doors, choosing instead to linger in the dimly lit material staging area where the engine noise never reached him. These intrusions appeared side by side in his routine, each demanding a different kind of caution. He had convinced himself that staying off the highways, skipping family gatherings where drinks were poured, and wearing heavy canvas gloves to dampen his grip were simply the necessary adjustments to keep his days steady. Over months, these adjustments hardened into habit. His wife, Leilani, took over the commute to their home in Waimanalo, and he found himself declining invitations to the church potlucks where his brothers still gathered. At the shop, he volunteered for the indoor assembly line, avoiding the bay doors entirely. The distance between him and his wife grew quiet and careful; she asked less about his days, and he stopped mentioning the tremors that lingered in his hands when a backfire echoed from a passing car. What finally brought him to this clinic was the way his own body had turned against him, the exhaustion of constantly bracing for an impact that had already passed. He sat across from the intake coordinator, his hands resting flat on his knees, and admitted that he was tired of navigating the world like a ghost in his own life. He had come to hope that someone might help him unclench his posture, trust the pavement again, and let the smell of rain be just rain, rather than a warning of a crash he could not outrun.
